records.text: ExposeSanAngelo — public records across Texas | ExposeTexas Skip to content The expansion queue Places we intend to cover next. These are not accusations. Each is on the list because of its structure — a large capital project, a dominant employer, fast growth, or a big incentive package — which is where public money concentrates and where the documents are worth reading. If something is wrong there, the records will show it. If nothing is wrong, the records will show that too, and we will publish it either way. Abilene & Taylor County Same West Texas water basin as San Angelo, same data-centre interest, same aquifer pressure. Know something here? → Midland & Odessa Permian Basin. Enormous property-tax abatements under Chapter 312/313-successor agreements. Know something here? → Lubbock Municipal electric utility and a fast-growing load from industrial siting. Know something here? → Waco & McLennan County Interstate-35 corridor development and rapid annexation. Know something here? → Tom Green County (beyond San Angelo) Appraisal-district valuations that set every tax bill in the county. Know something here? → Your town not listed? The queue is not a ranking and it is not fixed. A resident who knows what to ask for beats our guess about which county matters every time. Tell us what is happening where you live → You do not have to wait for us Texas's public records law covers every city, county, school district and state agency — not just the ones we have built a site for. The request we would file on your behalf is one you can file yourself today, and we will help you write it. Name a document, not a topic. “All agendas and minutes referencing X between these two dates” is hard to refuse. “Everything about X” invites a denial for being overly broad. Put the deadline in the letter. Citing the statute tells the custodian you know the clock is running. Ask for the exemption in writing. If they withhold, they must say which provision lets them. Escalate on paper. A refusal that exists in writing is the beginning of an appeal, not the end of a request. Use our request builder → About the Foundation

records.title: Watch your government
records.summary: Where to watch San Angelo government on video — meeting recordings, agendas, and the archives that keep them after the city takes them down.
records.text: Watch your government | ExposeTexas Skip to content MW A chapter of the Move Weight Foundation San Angelo, TX of 14 Oklahoma 4 Miami Oklahoma City Tulsa Claremore Texas 7 San Angelo Houston Dallas Austin San Antonio Lubbock Abilene Mississippi 3 Southaven Jackson Olive Branch All 14 chapters and the map → Video · San Angelo, TX Watch your government Almost every decision that costs you money is made in a room with a camera in it. The recordings are public. Most people never find them because they are buried three clicks deep on a government site. Here they are. Where the video lives San Angelo records City Council and posts to the City's own YouTube channel. Council meets 1st & 3rd Tuesday at 8:30 a.m. at the McNease Convention Center. City of San Angelo on YouTube City of San Angelo Official channel. Council meetings are streamed live here and to SATV (Optimum 17), FireTV and Roku. 411 recorded meetings indexed. Open → City Council meetings playlist City of San Angelo Every recorded Council meeting in one playlist — indexed and dated on our video archive. Open → Agendas, minutes & agenda packets City of San Angelo The packet usually contains the actual contract or ordinance under discussion. Open → We link, we do not rehost These are the government's own recordings on the government's own platforms. We send you there rather than mirroring them, so you are watching the authoritative copy and the view count lands where it belongs. The exception is when a recording disappears — see below. When a recording goes missing Meeting video gets taken down. Sometimes it is a retention policy, sometimes a platform migration, sometimes nobody can say why. Either way the public record evaporates, and the one meeting you needed is the one that is gone. That is why the Foundation's Miami, Oklahoma chapter keeps 522 meetings archived with machine transcripts and captions , mirrored to the Internet Archive. It is the deepest archive we run and the model for every other chapter. See what a full archive looks like → If you spot a gap A meeting with no video, a recording that ends mid-item, a link that used to work — tell us . A missing recording is itself a records request: the city holds the raw file whether or not it publishes it, and we will ask for it. Getting more out of a meeting recording Read the agenda packet first. It usually contains the actual contract or ordinance. The video is people discussing a document you can already have in front of you. Note the timestamp of anything that matters. A citation like "14 January, 1:42:10" is something a reporter or an auditor can verify in a minute. Watch the vote, not the speech. Who moved it, who seconded, who was absent, and whether it was on a published agenda. Executive session is a flag, not a crime. Bodies may close a meeting for defined reasons and must certify which. If a payment or a contract was discussed behind a closed door, the certification is a public record. Ask for it → Follow this chapter No social accounts yet. When the Foundation creates one for this chapter it is added to chapters/sanangelo.json and appears here and in the footer automatically. We publish to the site first. Social accounts are a distribution channel, never the record — anything we post there exists here with its source document attached.

records.summary: San Angelo
records.text: Water — what San Angelo actually has | ExposeTexas Skip to content Source Type Notes O.H. Ivie Reservoir Surface The chief surface source for meeting daily demand. Twin Buttes Reservoir Surface Part of the city's surface supply system. Concho River Surface Local surface water. Hickory Aquifer Groundwater Piped in from McCulloch County. Allocation rises to 10,000 acre-feet/yr in 2026 and 12,000 by 2036 . Operating strategy draws about 1.5 MGD as a required minimum. Current restriction level With roughly 41 months of supply, the City is in standard conservation : outside watering restricted to twice every seven days, no more than one inch per week. Those are the rules residents live under right now, before a single data center building exists. Source: City of San Angelo — Water Resources The $400 million plant Missing a timeline “may cost all of us lots of money.” Mayor Tom Thompson, defending the compressed data center timeline while citing $400 million needed for a new water treatment plant — SanAngeloLive, Dec. 31, 2025 This is the clearest statement of the city's actual logic: San Angelo needs an enormous capital investment in water infrastructure, and a $21–22 billion taxable facility is how the city hopes to pay for it. That is a coherent argument, and it deserves to be evaluated on the numbers rather than on vibes. Evaluating it requires three things the public does not currently have: the executed Chapter 380 agreement, a projection of campus water demand at full build-out, and the financing plan for the treatment plant showing which revenue actually retires which debt, in which years. We have records requests drafted for all three. File a request → See the budget side How the data center rules interact with the supply The June 16, 2026 water ordinance (adopted 7–0) sets these limits on any data center: Requirement Limit What it leaves open Cooling type Closed-loop only; no evaporative cooling This is the meaningful win. Evaporative cooling is what makes data centers water-hungry. Initial fill 8.0 gal / sq ft of gross building area Scales with building size, which the ordinance does not cap in total. Fill window Within 12 months of certificate of occupancy Phased buildings mean repeated fills across the build-out. Annual makeup 3% of loop volume per building Percentage of a volume that itself grows with each building. Drain and refill No more than every 3 years Each refill is effectively another initial fill. Metering Cooling water metered separately Good. Makes verification possible — if the readings are released. Source City municipal system, not on-site wells Means the campus competes with residents, not with itself. Chemicals Food-grade propylene glycol anticipated; no PFAS “added or allowed” Enforcement and testing regime not specified publicly. Sources: Water usage ordinance (PDF) · City of San Angelo — Data Center Information · SanAngeloLive Give the City its due Mandating closed-loop cooling and banning evaporative cooling is genuinely the strongest water protection available to a city in this position, and San Angelo adopted it unanimously. The criticism here is about sequence — the zoning was locked in five months before any of these rules existed — and about the absence of a published total-demand projection. It is not a claim that the ordinance is meaningless. Has this happened before? Yes. San Angelo has faced repeated water scarcity, and local reporting has asked directly whether another crisis is coming. The Hickory Aquifer pipeline itself was built as a response to that exposure — a multi-phase project stretching back over a decade. Further reading: SanAngeloLive — Will San Angelo Be Hit With Another Water Crisis? · Hickory Aquifer Project Moves Into New Phase · Concho Observer — Four Crucial Questions About San Angelo's Water
